title: Lost but Not Erased: Traces of a Forgotten Language in Neural Speech Models
hook: International adoptees keep traces of a birth language they can't speak. Train an ASR model on one language, switch it abruptly to another, and the same thing happens — no biology needed.
key_points: The study simulates the adoptee experience in ASR models: train on language A, abruptly switch to language B.
Traces of the first language persisted throughout second-language training, mainly in the lowest, pre-phonemic layers.
The traces are functional: early-exposure models re-learned their lost first language 14% faster than naive models.
The advantage held even against models 'adopted' early from a related language.
It disappeared when the earliest layers were swapped in from a non-adopted model — localizing the effect.
Authors argue critical periods reflect entrenchment of foundational representations, not maturational loss of plasticity.
content_html: International adoptees retain phonological traces of a birth language they can no longer speak or understand. The standard explanation is a biologically-timed critical period. Plantinga and colleagues test whether ordinary learning dynamics suffice — using automatic speech recognition models, which have no biology to appeal to.
extra_html:
The simulation

Models were trained on one language and then abruptly switched to a second, mimicking the adoptee experience without maturational confounds. Traces of the first language persisted throughout second-language training, concentrated mainly in the lowest, pre-phonemic layers — the parts of the network closest to raw acoustics.

The traces do work

Persistence alone would be a curiosity; the authors show the traces are functional. Models with early exposure re-learned their lost first language 14% faster than naive models. The advantage held even against models adopted early from a related language, ruling out generic linguistic similarity as the explanation. And it disappeared when the earliest layers were substituted from a non-adopted model — pinning the effect to exactly the layers where the traces were found. On that basis the authors argue critical-period effects reflect entrenchment of foundational representations rather than a maturational loss of plasticity, giving experience a central role in language acquisition's critical periods. A nice example of a neural network used as a controlled model organism for a cognitive-science question. arXiv, 2026.

related.title: Whisper: Robust Speech Recognition at Scale
related.hook: Train a plain encoder-decoder transformer on 680,000 hours of weakly-labeled multilingual audio and you get near-human transcription robustness without task-specific fine-tuning.

related.title: When Real Speech Is Off-Limits, RL Beats Fine-Tuning on Synthetic Audio
related.hook: Banks can't just collect real customer speech to adapt voice AI. Trained only on synthetic TTS audio, GRPO cuts word-error rate 40% more than supervised fine-tuning alone.

related.title: Small Models Are Enough to Imitate Human Choice Behaviour
related.hook: Fourteen models from 135M to 14B were fine-tuned on 10.7 million human decisions. In-distribution, 0.6B matched a 70B baseline — scale only started paying off on unfamiliar tasks.

flashcards.prompt: Why is an ASR model a useful stand-in for studying critical periods in language?
flashcards.back_html: It simulates the international-adoptee experience — abrupt switch from one language to another — without any maturational confound. Whatever persists can't be explained by a biological clock.

flashcards.prompt: Where in the network did traces of the abandoned first language persist?

choices.text: Mainly in the lowest, pre-phonemic layers
Mainly in the topmost output layers

flashcards.explanation_html: The localization is what makes the result testable: substituting the earliest layers from a non-adopted model made the re-learning advantage disappear.

flashcards.prompt: What alternative explanation for critical periods do the authors propose?
flashcards.back_html: Entrenchment of foundational representations formed by early experience — rather than a maturational loss of plasticity. Experience, not a biological clock, does much of the work.
